rule: Order 95-128 of 7 March 1995, Annex II, expressly excludes processed Camellia sinensis products from the plant-import prohibition. Annex III section 2.5 authorizes manufactured dried, roasted, candied and dehydrated plant products without a phytosanitary certificate when prepared so they present no quarantine-pest contamination risk and are not otherwise prohibited. They must be declared on entry. Section 2.1 imposes a permit on fresh/refrigerated fruit and vegetables, while section 2.5 imposes no permit on the manufactured category. Applying that category to clean, sealed, steamed/dried sencha supports the scoped shipment; this is a reasoned application of an express processing exemption.
personalMailApplicability: Article 8 of Order 95-128 applies its requirements to private postal imports. The manufactured-product exemption in Annex III section 2.5 is commodity-based and is not restricted to passenger baggage.

permitFreeReason: The operative annex expressly admits suitably processed dried plant products without a phytosanitary certificate and exempts processed tea from the tea-plant prohibition. No permit is prescribed for that category. Use only sealed, properly processed, pest-free pure sencha and make the ordinary arrival/postal declaration; fresh tea, propagative material and contaminated goods are outside this conclusion.

rule: Plant Protection and Quarantine Proclamation 1400/2026 is the current starting point, replacing reliance on the 1992 law. Processed products are covered where pest risk remains, and article 4 provides import controls; a current list resolving finished tea was not located.
personalMailApplicability: No personal postal tea exemption established under the new law.
remainingQuestion: What implementing commodity classification and personal postal exception apply to steamed tea under the 2026 proclamation?

rule: Law 02-013 article 2 covers plant products prepared by drying, grinding, shelling or pressing. Decree 02-305 article 6 requires every importer of plants/plant products to present an import permit; an origin phytosanitary certificate is additionally required where applicable. Article 8 expressly applies this pathway to postal consignments. Treat the scoped identifiable steamed/dried tea leaves as a dried plant product under that definition. This application is an inference from the explicit dried-product wording, not a published sencha-specific determination; steaming and retail packing do not by themselves establish an exemption.
personalMailApplicability: Decree 02-305 article 8 expressly covers post, and article 6 applies to every person importing covered products. No personal-use or small-parcel exception was established.

permitFreeReason: An import permit is required for dried plant products, including postal imports. Applying that explicit category to the dried sencha leaves is a stated inference. Because the store will not obtain permits, exclude this destination under the available rule; this is a documentary requirement, not an absolute tea ban.

rule: Law 14/PR/95 article 2(b) defines plant material broadly to include plant parts and objects manufactured from plants; this is separate from article 2(c), which also covers products simply prepared by drying. Article 16 subjects all plant material to import control, and article 18 requires an origin phytosanitary certificate for all articles covered by article 16. Applying the broad plant-material wording to identifiable steamed/dried sencha leaves is a reasoned inference. The separate approval for regular professional importers in article 17 is not automatically imposed on private consumers.
personalMailApplicability: The consignment-certificate requirement is not limited to professional importers. No small private postal exception was found in the reviewed law.
researchAttempts: Read articles 2 and 16–18; distinguished professional-activity approval from consignment certification and searched implementing exceptions.

Independently reread articles 2(b), 2(c) and 16–18. The broader plant-material definition, including manufactured plant objects, resolves the earlier unnecessary dependence solely on whether steaming is simple preparation. permitFreeReason: The broad plant-material definition includes plant parts and objects manufactured from plants; articles 16 and 18 require an origin phytosanitary certificate for that material. Applying this to the scoped dried leaves is an explicit inference. The store cannot satisfy the certificate requirement; tea is not thereby described as absolutely prohibited.

rule: Law 96-007 includes dried plant products, but articles 28–29 leave permits and accompanying documents subject to implementing prescriptions. Decree 98-099 articles 27–28 likewise defer the commodity conditions to ministerial orders. The operative Ministry-hosted fee order of 2 August 2011 expressly lists imported tea among foodstuffs subject to inspection, so processed tea cannot be assumed outside plant-health controls. That fee list does not itself establish which special document a 100 g private postal parcel needs. The official permit application accommodates postal entry, but a form alone does not prove that every inspected food needs a permit.
personalMailApplicability: The official permit form expressly accommodates postal imports; no general postal exemption is established. Whether that permit is required for the scoped tea has not been resolved by the published fee schedule or general law.

rule: Decree-Law 4/99 article 2(b) covers unprocessed plant products or products subjected to simple preparation. Articles 7–8 establish inspection and a prior import licence for covered goods. Unlike the explicit drying examples in several neighbouring laws, this definition does not specify the processing category that covers steamed/dried manufactured tea; no national commodity annex resolving it was located.
personalMailApplicability: No private-post exemption was found, but the commodity scope of the licensing rule for manufactured tea remains unverified.
